Junkyard Dog 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am Has the Great W72 Powertrain, It Will Make Grown Men Cry
36 photos
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society
Tucked between a mundane Chevrolet Impala and a weathered Buick Park Avenue in a sun-baked salvage yard, a stripped 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am rests precariously on stacked steel wheel rims. Documented by Benny Sanchez, the host of the Classic Ride Society YouTube channel, and avid derelict Detroit iron hunter, this battered coupe hides a remarkable secret beneath its peeling paint: a factory 400-cubic-inch, paired with a 4-speed manual drivetrain.
This junkyard inmate’s history can be traced back almost sixty years ago, with the debut of the Pontiac Firebird moniker. The Pontiac pony car was deliberately launched on 23 February 1967 as a corporate counterpart to Chevrolet's Camaro – and it was that precise reason that delayed the Firebird by five months.
GM wanted something to take on the Mustangs, and the Chevy Camaro was given the right of way, putting the Poncho in a cone shadow. Although it was one of the two true pony cars that soldiered on through the seventies (while the Mustang was a Pinto in disguise), the Firebird didn’t have the same public appeal as the Chevy.
Mind you, it wasn’t a poor-selling machine at all; it just wasn’t as good as the Camaro. Built across four generations over 36 model years, total Firebird production reached 2,614,563 units, comprising 277,380 first-generation cars from 1967 to 1969, 1,179,407 second-gens over 12 model years (1970 to 1981), 840,597vehicles between 1982 and 1992, and a final 317,179 production total for the fourth and final iteration (1993 to 2002).
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society In March 1969, two full years after the Firebird debuted, Pontiac introduced the Trans Am performance package, paying a $5 royalty per vehicle to the Sports Car Club of America for using its series name. Built across 34 model years from 1969 to 2002, Trans Am volumes totaled 927,210 units, consisting of 697 first-generation cars in 1969, 459,213 second-generation models, 332,480 third-generation cars, and 134,820 fourth-generation models produced through August 2002.
The 1979 model year marked the 10-year anniversary of the Trans Am moniker and brought freshly restyled urethane front fascias with quad rectangular headlamps alongside full-width slotted taillights. Despite tightening emissions standards and rising fuel costs, 1979 set an all-time Firebird production record of 211,453 cars, divided by model into 38,642 base Firebirds, 30,853 luxury Esprits including 4,248 Redbird editions, 24,850 twin-scoop Formulas, and a record 117,108 Trans Am coupes.
Coincidence or not, the Camaro also sold its all-time best volumes (282,582 ponies). It was also the year of the fox-body Mustang, which absolutely crashed the Chevy-Poncho party and completely stole the show with 369,936 debuting third-gen cars.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society For 1979, the cheapest Trans Am carried a base price of $6,299 and came standard with the RPO L80 403-cubic-inch (advertised in the traditional Pontiac European spelling “6.6-litre”) Oldsmobile four-barrel V8 paired with the RPO MX1 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 350 automatic transmission.
Breathing through a reverse-mounted shaker hood scoop, that standard Olds engine was good for 185 horsepower at 3,600 rpm and 315 lb-ft-ft of torque at 2,000 rpm, and it came exclusively with an automatic transmission.
Two optional V8s and an extra-cost manual gearbox completed the 1979 Trans Am lineup. Buyers prioritizing fuel economy could specify the RPO L37 301-cuber, Pontiac’s 4.9-liter, four-barrel V8, rated at 150 horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 240 lb-ft at 2,000 rpm, which provided a $150 credit and could be mated to either the standard 3-speed automatic transmission or the no-cost optional RPO M21 close-ratio 4-speed manual transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Enthusiasts demanding maximum performance ordered the RPO W72 motor, Pontiac’s true apex predator: 400-cubic-inch (marked with “T/A 6.6” on the hood scoop) Pontiac single-quad V8. PMD actually stockpiled whatever 400 blocks it could at the end of 1978 for one final glorious anniversary run.
Rated at 220 horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 320 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm, the $90 optional 400-incher required the no-cost Borg-Warner Super T-10 4-speed manual transmission and the mandatory $434 WS6 Special Performance Package, adding $524 to a standard Trans Am sticker.
Breaking down the 117,108 Trans Ams built for 1979 reveals how buyers configured their cars across four sub-models and two transmissions. Overall, 105,449 customers chose the 3-speed automatic transmission, while only 11,659 selected the 4-speed manual gearbox.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Body-wise, Pontiac produced 59,578 standard hardtop coupes, 38,476 T-Tops with the $655 CC1 removable glass panels, 11,554 Y84 Black Special Edition coupes ($1,329 extra), and 7,500 Y89 TATAs (Tenth Anniversary Trans Am) coupes, priced at an eyewatering $10,619.
Separating those 117,108 Trans Ams by engine and transmission highlights the scarcity of manual-shift cars. The standard 403 V8 and automatic transmission powered 94,773 examples, comprising 48,488 hardtop coupes, 30,728 T-Top coupes, 9,874 Black Special Editions, and 5,683 10th Anniversary editions.
The 301 V8 accounted for 14,009 cars, split into 7,015 automatic and 1,590 manual hardtops, 3,301 automatic and 1,530 manual T-Tops, and 360 automatic and 213 manual Special Editions.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society That leaves just 8,326 Trans Ams, alongside 346 Formulas, equipped with the W72 400-cubic-inch Pontiac V8 and 4-speed manual transmission in 1979. Across the four Trans Am sub-models, Pontiac built 2,485 hardtop coupes, 1,107 Y84 Black Special Editions, 1,817 Y89 10th Anniversary models, and 2,917 T-Tops. This junkyard find is one of those 2,917 T-Top 400 4-speeds (that’s 2.49 percent of the grand total of Trans Ams).
Built on the fourth week of October 1978, and sprayed in Heritage Brown Metallic paint with the $150 Camel cloth interior, this sore sight for nostalgic eyes was quite the brawler back in its heyday. Truth be told, that 220-hp rating was a bit downplayed – real-world testing placed it closer to 260 net, which was about the best thing money could buy in 1979.
Just for reference, America’s Sportscar, the Corvette, offered a 225-horse 350-cube small-block V8 as the top dog. The Trans Am, naturally, couldn’t take the spotlight away from GM’s favorite child – in brochures, at least – but it sure had it its way on the street. Well, that’s all long gone now, with this boneyard dog having made peace with the thought that the only way out of there is though the smelting furnace.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Decades of neglect in the elements have taken a heavy toll on the Heritage Brown Metallic bodywork. With the shaker hood, carburetor, valve covers, and exhaust long gone, rainwater has pooled inside the venerable 400 V8 block. Previous scavengers have already stripped the slotted rear taillights, cracked the rear decklid spoiler, and removed the wheels.
Despite the missing 15x8-inch aluminum Snowflake wheels, which the car hunter now kicks himself for passing up years ago when they were around $300, the undercarriage retains unmistakable WS6 Special Performance Package hardware. Rusted rotors and calipers on all four corners confirm the factory J65 4-wheel power disc brakes, complemented by a thick front sway bar and front wheel spoilers he plans to salvage for his own 1977 Firebird Formula, and vintage Rocket traction bars.
Both doors remain jammed shut, and even a pair of bolt cutters borrowed from a nearby pickup bed fails to pry the driver latch open. Peering through the shattered window glass and open T-Top roof reveals a loose tilt steering column, sun-baked Camel Tan hobnail cloth seats draped in tattered sheepskin covers, an empty 1987 Roger Troutman cassette case, and the chrome Hurst shifter handle of that 4-speed manual transmission.
Speaking of which, the original Borg-Warner Super T-10 cogbox and its three linkage rods remain bolted ahead of the 3.23:1 Safe-T-Track limited-slip rear axle. Although severe rust and missing body panels have pushed this rare 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am beyond any hope, its powertrain components still await rescue before the crusher claims another legend.
